name: Marmaris
desc: A yacht town wrapped around a bay so enclosed the water stays flat, with pine hills dropping straight into it and a small castle on the knoll above the old quarter. The marina end is superyachts and gelato; ten minutes west the back lanes still have stone houses, a bazaar and charcoal fish grills.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — July and August are hot, packed and loud until 4am
tip: Skip the seafront strip and eat in the lanes behind the castle, then take the water taxi to Turunç rather than swimming off the town beach.
todo: Old town lanes below the castle
Fish market grill in the bazaar
rev: Visitors like the sheltered bay, the boat trips and the value, and complain in the same breath about the wall of bars on Bar Street, restaurant touts and a town beach that is more marina than sand.
onward: Dalaman (DLM) airport, then about 90 minutes by road or the Havaş bus; Bodrum (BJV) is a longer 2.5-hour drive

name: Marmaris Castle
desc: A small Ottoman fortress rebuilt by Süleyman the Magnificent before the siege of Rhodes, sitting on the rock the old town climbs. Inside are seven rooms of amphorae, ship models and Carian finds around a courtyard of bougainvillea; the real value is the wall-walk, which looks down on the harbour, the tiled roofs and the whole bay.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the courtyard bakes at midday in summer
tip: Come in the last hour before closing, when the light hits the bay and the cruise groups have gone back down the hill.
rev: People find the museum itself modest and over quickly, but almost everyone says the ramparts and the walk up through the old lanes justify the small ticket.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then 90 minutes to Marmaris; the castle is a five-minute walk uphill from the marina

name: Turunç
desc: A single crescent of coarse pale sand and very clear deep water under steep pine ridges, twenty winding kilometres south of Marmaris. It stays small because the road is a chain of hairpins, and the sea shelves fast, which makes it a swimmer's beach rather than a paddler's one.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming; May and Oct are quiet and still warm enough
tip: Take the hourly water taxi from Marmaris instead of driving — the road is beautiful but the village car parks fill by ten in August.
todo: Swim off the rocks at the south end
rev: Regulars rate the water quality above anything near Marmaris; the recurring gripes are the hairpin road, sunbed charges on most of the sand and how little happens after dinner.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), 90 min to Marmaris, then 20 km of hairpins or the water taxi from the harbour

name: Amos
desc: A small Rhodian-period town on the headland above Kumlubük, with a theatre cut into the slope and its seats still facing the bay. There is a stretch of polygonal wall, a temple terrace and inscriptions about land leases; a ten-minute path from the road gets you there and you usually have it to yourself.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — no shade, and the path is slippery after rain
tip: Climb to the top row of the theatre and sit down — the sea fills the whole stage opening, which is the entire reason to come.
rev: Almost everyone calls it the best-value ruin near Marmaris precisely because nobody is there, while noting the site is small, unlabelled and reached by a rough track that ordinary hire cars manage slowly.
onward: Dalaman (DLM) then Marmaris; from Turunç take the Kumlubük road and look for the sign above the bay

name: Marmaris National Park
desc: Thirty thousand hectares of red pine and sweetgum wrapping the peninsulas either side of Marmaris, with forest roads climbing to viewpoints over Hisarönü and Gökova. Wild boar and jackals are common, tortoises cross the tracks, and these pine forests are why Muğla supplies most of the country's pine honey.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — high fire risk closes forest roads in July and August
tip: Drive up to the Cennet Adası viewpoint above İçmeler at the end of the day, and check first, because the forestry barriers close on high-fire-risk days.
todo: Pine honey from a roadside stall
Walk a stretch of the Carian Trail
rev: Walkers praise the empty forest tracks and the smell of pine after rain, and report unsigned junctions, no water on the trails and closures after summer fires.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Marmaris; a car is essential — the trailheads are 10–30 km from town with no bus

name: Hisarönü Bay and Keçi Bükü
desc: The long shallow inlet on the north side of the Bozburun peninsula, with Keçi Bükü at its head: a wooded islet carrying a Byzantine fort, a line of gulets on the mooring buoys and shallows that turn the water milky green. Marmaris is half an hour away and it feels like a different decade.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — the meltemi funnels hard down the bay in July and August
tip: Hire a kayak at Keçi Bükü and paddle out to the fort islet; there is no jetty, so aim for the shingle on its north side.
near: Keçi Bükü, Orhaniye, Marmaris, Muğla, Türkiye
todo: Kayak to the Byzantine fort islet
Fish lunch on the Keçi Bükü jetty
rev: Sailors rate it as the best shelter on this coast, while swimmers find it weedy and shallow, with jellyfish in late summer and almost no beach.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Marmaris and 25 km west on the Bozburun road; dolmuşes run to Orhaniye but not late

name: Kızkumu (Orhaniye's Sunken Road)
desc: A 600-metre spit of red gravel lying just under the surface, so you walk out into the middle of the bay with water at your knees and the shore a long way behind you. The legend involves a princess carrying sand in her skirt; the geology involves a submerged ridge. Mountains close in on three sides.
season: May–Oct — outside that the water is too cold to enjoy the walk
tip: Walk it early or late: at midday the shallow water is bath-warm with no shade, and stepping off the edge of the spit drops you into six metres.
todo: Walk the full spit at sunset
Fish restaurant on the Orhaniye shore
Bybassos ruins on the hill above
rev: Families love the novelty and the safe shallow water; complaints centre on sharp gravel underfoot, access through waterfront restaurants that expect an order, and a car park full by mid-morning.
entry: Free — most access is through restaurants that expect an order
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Marmaris and 20 km on the Bozburun road; dolmuş from Marmaris otogar to Orhaniye

name: Selimiye
desc: A boatbuilding village on the Bozburun peninsula that became a quiet harbour of stone houses, jasmine and fish restaurants without acquiring a single tall building. There are remains of a Hellenistic watchtower on the hill behind, and a swim platform at the end of the jetty that locals use at dawn.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — most restaurants shut from November to March
tip: Book a waterfront table the day before in August, and ask what came in that morning rather than ordering off the printed menu.
todo: Swim off the jetty at first light
Walk up to the Hellenistic tower
rev: Visitors describe it as what Marmaris was forty years ago, and warn that prices are now Bodrum-level, there is no proper beach and the single road in is narrow.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Marmaris and 40 km of winding road; dolmuşes run Marmaris–Bozburun via Selimiye several times a day

name: Bozburun
desc: The last working gulet-building town: hulls the size of houses sit on the slipways at the edge of the harbour and the whole waterfront smells of pine resin and varnish. There is no beach, which is why it stayed a village of sponge divers and boatwrights with a handful of pensions on the water.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — winter here is genuinely closed
tip: Walk the shore road south past the yards towards Söğüt for the view back across the bay, and buy sponge or thyme honey directly from the harbour stalls.
todo: Watch a gulet hull being planked
Thyme honey from a harbour stall
Boat out to Kızıl Ada to swim
rev: Travellers who want quiet rate it highly and those expecting a resort are disappointed: no sand, little nightlife, and 50 km of bends from Marmaris that take well over an hour.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Marmaris and 50 km southwest; dolmuş from Marmaris otogar roughly every two hours in summer

name: Loryma (Bozukkale)
desc: A Hellenistic fortress at the tip of the peninsula, nine towers of dressed limestone still standing above a fjord-shaped inlet where Athenian and Rhodian fleets once sheltered. There is no proper road, so it is either a long walk from Söğüt or a yacht anchorage, and most days it is you and the goats.
season: Apr–May and Oct — no shade, no water, and the walk is brutal in summer
tip: Carry all your water: the track from Söğüt passes no spring, and the single seasonal shack at the anchorage may not be open.
rev: Sailors and walkers call it one of the most atmospheric ruins on the coast, and everyone warns that the final dirt road destroys ordinary cars and that there is no shade, water or signage.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Marmaris to Söğüt by dolmuş and a 6 km walk; most people arrive by gulet or on a Bozburun day boat

name: Eski Datça
desc: The stone village the modern town grew out of, two kilometres inland: single-storey houses in unrendered rubble stone, bougainvillea over the lanes, almond and olive trees between the walls. The poet Can Yücel lived and is buried here, which is why the cafés play a certain kind of music and the bookshop is better than it needs to be.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — February almond blossom is the local secret
tip: Come for breakfast rather than dinner: the courtyard places serve almond dessert and village eggs before the day-trippers walk up from the harbour.
rev: Visitors love the lanes and the shade, and note that it is small enough to see in an hour, that prices are high for what it is, and that August evenings fill it with coaches.
onward: Dalaman (DLM) then 2.5 hours by road, or the summer Bodrum (BJV) ferry to Datça; the old village is 3 km up from the harbour

name: Knidos
desc: A city built on the very tip of the peninsula where two seas meet, with twin harbours, a round temple terrace that once held Praxiteles' Aphrodite, and a theatre facing the strait to Kos. The wind never stops, the marble is white against blue on three sides, and the last 35 km of road is the price of admission.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — fully exposed, with no shade anywhere on site
tip: Walk up to the round temple platform first thing; the afternoon boats from Datça all arrive together and that terrace is where everyone stands.
rev: People rate the setting above the ruins themselves and consistently complain about the long, slow, partly rough road from Datça, the total lack of shade and the wind.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Datça and 35 km west on a slow single-track road; summer day boats from Datça harbour avoid the drive

name: Palamutbükü
desc: A kilometre of white pebble on the peninsula's south coast, backed by a row of fish restaurants and almond terraces instead of hotels. The water is startlingly clear because there is no sand to stir up, and Rhodes sits on the horizon. Ovabükü and Hayıtbükü, the next coves east, are the same idea in miniature.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming; May and Oct are warm but many places shut
tip: Park at the west end by the fishing harbour rather than on the restaurant strip, and bring water shoes — the pebbles are large and the entry is sharp.
todo: Swim off the pebbles at the west end
rev: Repeat visitors praise the water clarity and the absence of concrete, and grumble about sunbed prices, restaurants fencing off most of the beach, and 25 km of bends from Datça.
entry: Free — sunbeds charged by the restaurants
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Datça and 25 km over the ridge on a good but twisting road; dolmuş twice a day in summer

name: Datça Peninsula Road
desc: Seventy-five kilometres from the Marmaris junction to Knidos along a ridge with the Gulf of Gökova on one side and the Hisarönü gulf on the other, through almond groves, beehives and the isthmus at Balıkaşıran where the two seas are 800 metres apart. The final stretch to Knidos is single-track and slow.
season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — February almond blossom turns the whole ridge white
tip: Stop at the Balıkaşıran isthmus where both gulfs are visible from one layby, and fill the tank in Datça, because there is no fuel west of it.
rev: Drivers call it one of the best roads in the country and warn about slow coaches, blind bends, goats on the tarmac and a final section to Knidos rough enough to punish a low car.
onward: Dalaman (DLM) or Bodrum (BJV); collect the car at the airport, the peninsula road begins at the Marmaris–Muğla junction near Gökova

name: Carian Trail
desc: An 800-kilometre waymarked path through old Caria, looping the Bozburun and Datça peninsulas and the shores of the Gulf of Gökova. Unlike the Lycian Way it strings together ruins nobody stops at — Hydas, Bybassos, Loryma — and long stretches run on goat paths through pine and carob with the sea far below.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — summer is dangerously hot and water sources dry up
tip: Walk the Bozburun peninsula section in April, when the cisterns still hold water and the village pensions at Selimiye and Söğüt have opened for the season.
rev: Walkers rate the emptiness and the ruins highly, and repeatedly report faded waymarks, overgrown sections, unreliable water and villages where the only shop closed years ago.
onward: Dalaman (DLM) or Bodrum (BJV), then dolmuş to Marmaris, Bozburun or Datça for the main trailheads

name: Akyaka
desc: A village of white timber-fronted houses in the local Nail Çakırhan style at the head of the Gökova gulf, where a cold spring river meets the sea. Pine ridges rise straight behind it, the wind funnels down the gulf every afternoon, and a Cittaslow charter keeps the buildings low.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — the meltemi turns July and August into a kitesurfing season
tip: Take a flat-bottomed boat up the Azmak river at dusk to watch the springs boiling up through the weed and the kingfishers working; it beats the beach comfortably.
rev: Visitors love the river, the architecture and the fish restaurants, and complain about the relentless afternoon wind, a small crowded beach and August weekend traffic from İzmir.
onward: Dalaman (DLM) about 90 minutes, or Bodrum (BJV) about the same; Muğla–Marmaris buses stop at the Akyaka junction on the ridge

name: Sedir Island (Cleopatra Beach)
desc: A small island in the Gökova gulf carrying the ruins of Kedrai — a theatre, a city wall, temple foundations — and a beach of near-spherical white ooid grains found almost nowhere else in the Mediterranean. The sand is fenced off: you may not lie on it or carry a grain away, and wardens actually check.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — the daily boats stop running by November
tip: Shower in the marked area before leaving; removing sand is prosecuted, and the beach closes to swimmers when the wardens judge the crowd too large.
rev: The water and the ruins get consistent praise, but many find the sand rules heavy-handed, the island small enough for an hour, and the boats delivering everyone at once from Çamlı.
entry: ≈€6 island fee plus the boat fare from Çamlı or Akyaka
onward: Dalaman (DLM) or Bodrum (BJV), then Çamlı harbour near Akyaka for the 20-minute boat; Marmaris day trips also run

name: Lake Köyceğiz
desc: A large brackish lake joined to the sea by the Dalyan channel and ringed by sweetgum forest, the liquidambar that grows at this scale nowhere else. The water is warm, shallow and faintly sulphurous at the south end, and the lakefront at Köyceğiz town is a mile of plane trees and almost empty promenade.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — mosquitoes are serious on summer evenings
tip: Take the public boat from Köyceğiz town down the channel to Dalyan rather than a tour: the same route, a third of the price, and it calls at Sultaniye.
rev: People find the town refreshingly untouristed and the lake beautiful at dawn; the standard complaints are mosquitoes, a muddy lake bottom and boatmen quoting three different prices.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), 45 minutes by road; all Marmaris–Fethiye buses stop at Köyceğiz otogar, five minutes from the lakefront

name: Sultaniye Hot Springs
desc: Sulphur water at around 39 °C rising on the south-west shore of Lake Köyceğiz, fed into an open pool and a domed Ottoman bath beside a small shrine. The mud pit next door is the same idea as Dalyan's with far fewer people, and you rinse off in the lake afterwards.
season: Oct–May is the sweet spot — 39 °C water in August is unpleasant
tip: Arrive by boat from Köyceğiz in the morning ahead of the Dalyan day-trip flotilla, and bring an old swimsuit, because the sulphur stains fabric permanently.
todo: Soak in the domed Ottoman bath
Walk to the shrine and its plane tree
rev: Bathers report the water genuinely helps aching joints, and warn about the powerful sulphur smell, basic changing rooms and midday crowds off the tour boats.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Köyceğiz; boats run from the town quay, or drive 25 km round the west shore on a partly unpaved road

name: Dalyan
desc: A river town where flat-bottomed boats thread reed channels between lake and sea, with the Lycian rock tombs of Kaunos carved into the cliff directly opposite the restaurant terraces. Loggerhead turtles come up the river to the fish weirs, and because the whole delta is protected, no hotel rises more than a few floors.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — July and August are hot and the boat queues long
tip: Use the little co-operative rowing ferry across to the tombs and the Kaunos path instead of booking a boat tour; it runs all day for the price of a coffee.
rev: Visitors love the river, the tombs and the turtles, and complain about identical boat tours sold by every stall, mosquitoes at dusk and a main street that is now solid restaurants.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), 25 minutes by road — the shortest airport hop on this coast; dolmuş from Ortaca every half hour

name: Kaunos
desc: A Carian city that died when its harbour silted into marsh, leaving a theatre cut into the hillside, a Roman bath, a temple terrace and a Byzantine basilica standing above the reeds. The famous temple-façade rock tombs are half a kilometre downstream in the cliff, and are best seen from the water.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — exposed site, and the marsh breeds mosquitoes in summer
tip: Climb to the acropolis above the theatre for the view over the delta to İztuzu; hardly anyone goes up, and it is the only place the geography makes sense.
todo: Rock tombs seen from the river
rev: Most people rate the setting and the emptiness highly; the repeated complaints are a steep unshaded climb, mosquitoes near the marsh and rock tombs you cannot enter.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Dalyan; take the rowing ferry across the river and walk 20 minutes, or drive round via Çandır

name: İztuzu Beach
desc: A four-and-a-half kilometre sandbar separating the Dalyan delta from the open sea, river on one side and Mediterranean on the other. It is a loggerhead nesting beach, so it closes at eight in the evening, umbrellas are restricted to marked zones, and nothing has ever been built on it.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming; May and Oct are quiet with the turtle rules still in force
tip: Arrive by river boat at the far end rather than driving to the road entrance — the eastern half has the same sand and a fraction of the people.
todo: Walk the sandbar end to end
Turtle rescue centre at the river end
Swim on the river side at dusk
rev: Nearly everyone calls it the best undeveloped beach on the coast, then mentions the eight o'clock closure, the scarcity of shade and the trek from car park to water.
entry: Free — small parking fee at the road entrance
onward: Dalaman (DLM) 30 minutes to Dalyan, then the river boat or 13 km of road around the delta; a summer dolmuş runs

name: Yuvarlakçay
desc: A spring-fed stream north-east of Köyceğiz running under plane trees so dense the water stays green and cold through August. Trout restaurants sit on platforms over the current, otters live in the banks, and villagers camped out for months to stop a hydro plant being built on it.
season: Jun–Sep — the shade and the cold water are the whole point; winter is muddy
tip: Go on a weekday: at summer weekends every platform table is booked by families from Muğla and Denizli, and the road in is single lane.
todo: Trout lunch on a platform over the water
Cold swim under the plane trees
rev: Visitors describe it as the coolest place in the province in August, and note that the restaurants are interchangeable and pricey, the parking chaotic and the water genuinely cold.
entry: Free — the restaurants expect an order
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Köyceğiz and 12 km east on the Beyobası road; no bus, so drive or take a taxi

name: Göcek
desc: A one-street town at the head of a gulf so sheltered that six marinas fit around it, with pine mountains coming down to the water. There is no beach worth the name and that is deliberate: Göcek exists for the boats, the chandleries and the twelve islands scattered across the gulf in front of it.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — the gulet season either side of the August peak
tip: You do not need to charter: the public taxi boats from the town quay run a fixed circuit of the bays each morning for a fraction of the day-tour price.
todo: Morning taxi boat to Bedri Rahmi bay
Sunset from the Göcek tunnel viewpoint
rev: Sailors and repeat visitors love the anchorages and the low-key main street; the recurring complaints are marina prices, the absence of a real beach and how completely it empties in winter.
onward: Dalaman (DLM) is 20 minutes away, the shortest transfer on this coast; Fethiye is 25 km on through the tunnel

name: Twelve Islands
desc: The archipelago in the Gulf of Göcek: Tersane with its abandoned Greek village and derelict shipyard, Yassıca with a sandbar you can walk across, Domuz with its private jetties, and Bedri Rahmi bay, where the painter left a fish on a rock in 1973. Every one of them has clear deep water.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — August fills the anchorages and the meltemi builds after noon
tip: Ask the skipper to reach Bedri Rahmi's painted rock before eleven; after that four gulets moor in front of it and the fish is invisible from the water.
near: Tersane Adası, Göcek, Fethiye, Muğla, Türkiye
rev: Day-trippers rate the water and the empty ruins highly, and complain that standard tours allow twenty minutes per stop, that the included lunch is mediocre and that August anchorages are crowded.
entry: Free — you pay for the boat
onward: Dalaman (DLM), 20 minutes to Göcek; boats leave the town quay around 10am, or charter a small boat with a skipper

name: Fethiye
desc: A harbour town rebuilt after the 1957 earthquake, so the fabric is plain — the setting is not. A broad bay full of islands, Lycian sarcophagi standing between apartment blocks, rock tombs above the roofline, and a fish market where you buy the fish and the surrounding restaurants cook it for a fixed price.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the town works year-round, unlike Ölüdeniz
tip: At the fish market, choose from the stalls in the middle and hand it to any of the restaurants around them; the cooking charge per head is posted on the wall.
todo: Buy and cook at the fish market
rev: Long-stayers rate the market, the marina walk and the year-round life; complaints focus on a scruffy town beach at Çalış, heavy coast-road traffic and persistent timeshare touts.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), 50 minutes by road with a Havaş bus meeting most flights; long-distance buses run to İzmir and Antalya

name: Tomb of Amyntas
desc: A temple façade cut into the cliff above Fethiye in the 4th century BC: two Ionic columns, a pediment and a false door with iron studs rendered in stone, reached by a long flight of steps from the town. A Greek inscription names Amyntas son of Hermapias, and the whole bay opens out from the platform.
season: Year-round; avoid the climb between noon and four in summer
tip: Go up for sunset, when the rock turns orange and the tomb is floodlit from below, and pay at the kiosk rather than following the goat paths locals use.
todo: Climb the steps at golden hour
rev: Visitors call the façade and the view worth the steps, while noting that you cannot go inside, the site is small for the fee, and the staircase is steep with no handrail in places.
onward: Dalaman (DLM) then Fethiye; the steps start a 15-minute walk uphill from the harbour, signposted off Kaya Caddesi

name: Kayaköy
desc: Around 350 roofless stone houses on a hillside, emptied in the 1923 population exchange when the Greek-speaking Orthodox inhabitants left and nobody moved in. Two basilicas keep fragments of painted plaster and pebble mosaic floors, the lanes are cobbled and stepped, and the silence at the top of the village is the point.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the hillside is punishing in July and August
tip: Walk in from the top gate and come down through the village, then take the old mule path over the ridge to Ölüdeniz — about two hours, downhill at the end.
rev: Most people find it genuinely moving and quiet, and note the loose cobbles, the complete absence of shade and a ticket that surprises those who remember when it was free.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Fethiye and a 20-minute dolmuş from the Ölüdeniz stand; the last one back leaves early evening

name: Ölüdeniz
desc: The lagoon everyone has seen on a poster: a hooked spit of white shingle enclosing water that goes from clear to turquoise to deep blue within twenty metres, with Babadağ rising 1,900 metres directly behind. The lagoon is a protected nature park with nothing built on it; the resort strip sits round the corner on Belcekız beach.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — August is very hot and the beach is shoulder to shoulder
tip: Pay the small nature-park fee and go through to the lagoon proper instead of staying on the free Belcekız side: calmer water, and the paragliders land on the other beach.
rev: The colour of the water gets universal praise; the complaints are relentless — sunbed prices, crowds by ten in the morning, sharp shingle underfoot and a resort strip with no charm.
entry: ≈₺150 (≈€3.50) for the lagoon nature park; Belcekız beach is free
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Fethiye and a 25-minute dolmuş that runs every few minutes in season

name: Babadağ
desc: The 1,969-metre mountain behind Ölüdeniz and one of the most reliable paragliding sites anywhere: the takeoff ramps sit at roughly 1,700 and 1,965 metres and the glide down over the lagoon lasts half an hour. A cable car now runs to the top, so you can take the view and the summit terrace without jumping off anything.
season: Apr–Oct for flying; the cable car runs most of the year but wind closes it
tip: Book the first flight of the morning — the air is smoothest before ten, and by afternoon the thermals turn it rough enough that queasy passengers regret it.
todo: Tandem flight from the 1,965 m ramp
Cable car for the view alone
rev: Flyers call it the highlight of the trip, with common warnings about wind cancellations, hard sell on video packages and a bumpy jeep ride up if you fly rather than ride the cable car.
entry: Cable car ≈€25 return; tandem flights ≈€90–130 depending on the ramp
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Fethiye and the Ölüdeniz dolmuş; the cable car base station is at the inland end of the Ölüdeniz valley

name: Butterfly Valley
desc: A steep-sided gorge dropping to a shingle beach, reachable only by boat from Ölüdeniz or a rope-assisted scramble down from Faralya. Jersey tiger moths breed here in summer, there is a waterfall an hour up the valley bed, and the accommodation at the bottom is bungalows and hammocks rather than hotels.
season: Jun–Sep for the moths and the boats; the descent path is dangerous when wet
tip: Take the last boat back or stay the night — day-trippers get ninety minutes, and the valley only becomes itself after the four o'clock boat leaves.
todo: Walk up the valley to the waterfall
rev: People love the beach once the boats leave, and repeatedly warn that the cliff path from Faralya has killed walkers, that facilities are basic and that the moths are strictly seasonal.
entry: ≈€10 boat return from Ölüdeniz plus a small valley fee
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Fethiye and Ölüdeniz; boats leave the Belcekız beach jetty several times a day in season

name: Kabak Bay and Faralya
desc: The last habitable notch on this coast before the cliffs take over. Faralya sits on the ridge with the Lycian Way running through it; Kabak is the bay 400 metres below, reached by a shuttle or a steep 45-minute path. Treehouse camps, no hotels, and no road down onto the beach itself.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — most camps close from November to March
tip: Do not attempt the descent to Kabak in flip-flops or after dark: the tractor shuttles stop in the evening and the path is loose scree in places.
todo: Lycian Way to Butterfly Valley rim
rev: Walkers and long-stayers rate the quiet and the star-filled nights, while noting basic plumbing, patchy electricity, cash-only camps and 25 km of continuous bends on the road in.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Fethiye and the Ölüdeniz–Faralya dolmuş, roughly every two hours in summer and twice a day in winter

name: Gemiler Island
desc: An island covered end to end with a 5th–6th century Christian settlement: four basilicas, cisterns, tombs and a vaulted processional way climbing to a church on the summit. Some argue it was the original burial place of St Nicholas. You land at a jetty, pay a small fee and walk up through the whole thing.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — no shade, and the boats stop in winter
tip: The vaulted covered walkway on the north side is what most day-trippers miss, because it starts behind the second basilica rather than at the jetty.
todo: Swim off the island's north side
rev: Visitors find it far more substantial than expected, and warn about sharp loose stone underfoot, no shade or water on the island, and boat tours that allow barely an hour ashore.
entry: ≈€5 landing fee plus the boat from Ölüdeniz or Karacaören
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Fethiye; boats go from Ölüdeniz and from the Gemiler beach road below Kayaköy

name: Saklıkent Gorge
desc: An eighteen-kilometre slot cut through the Akdağ massif, entered on a boardwalk pinned to the wall above the river. Where the boardwalk ends you wade an icy blue torrent coming straight out of the mountain, then walk upstream between walls two hundred metres high that narrow to a few metres apart.
season: May–Oct; snowmelt flood closes the gorge from November to April
tip: Rent the rubber shoes at the entrance and go early — by midday the first ford is a queue, and the water is genuinely too cold to stand in for long.
todo: Trout lunch on the river platforms
Walk the boardwalk at opening time
rev: Most people call the first kilometre spectacular and then complain about the cold water, the crowded boardwalk, the stalls at the entrance and tour buses arriving in convoy from Fethiye.
entry: ≈₺200 (≈€5) national park entry; not covered by the Museum Pass
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Fethiye and 45 km east via Kemer; day tours usually combine it with Tlos

name: Tlos
desc: One of the oldest Lycian cities, stacked on a bluff over the Xanthos valley with an Ottoman governor's fortress on top of the acropolis and rock tombs cut into the cliff below it, including one with Bellerophon riding Pegasus carved beside the door. The theatre below is large, well preserved and faces the mountains.
season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — the valley is very hot in midsummer
tip: Bellerophon's tomb is reached by an unmarked scramble off the left of the fortress path; ask the ticket seller to point out where it starts.
todo: Bellerophon relief on the rock tomb
Stadium and baths below the bluff
rev: Visitors rate it the best-value ruin in the valley thanks to the setting, while mentioning the steep unmarked scramble to the tombs, thin signage and midday heat with no shade.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Fethiye and 35 km southeast via Kemer; usually combined with Saklıkent, 12 km further on

name: Pinara
desc: A Lycian city under a vertical cliff honeycombed with hundreds of rectangular tomb openings, cut so high they can only have been reached on ropes. Below, oaks grow through a theatre that still has its stage building, and the Royal Tomb carries a relief of a walled city. Cattle graze between the ruins.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the access track is bad after winter rain
tip: The last two kilometres are steep gravel switchbacks, so leave a low car in the village and walk up, and allow two hours because the site is spread through woodland.
todo: Pigeonhole tombs in the cliff face
rev: Those who make it call it the most atmospheric site in Lycia because they were alone; the consistent warnings are the rough access road, overgrown paths, snakes in summer and no facilities at all.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Fethiye and 45 km south on the D400 to Minare village; a high-clearance car helps on the final climb

name: Letoon
desc: The federal sanctuary of the Lycian League: three temples side by side to Leto, Apollo and Artemis on a plain where the water table has risen so far that half the site is now a pond full of frogs and terrapins. The trilingual stele found here, in Lycian, Greek and Aramaic, is how the Lycian language was cracked.
season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — the flooded section is deepest after winter rain
tip: Come late in the afternoon when the columns reflect in the standing water; that reflection is the photograph and it does not work at midday.
todo: Three temple foundations side by side
rev: People find it small but unusually atmospheric, and note the flooding, the mosquitoes, the modest theatre and the fact that the famous stele is in Fethiye museum rather than on site.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Fethiye and about an hour southeast via Eşen to Kumluova; no useful bus, so drive

name: Cadyanda
desc: A Lycian hill city at 1,000 metres above Üzümlü, set in pine forest with a stadium, a theatre, baths and a paved road still showing cart ruts. The loop path runs under trees, which makes it the one Lycian site you can walk at midday in July, and the view drops all the way to Fethiye bay.
season: May–Oct; the access road can be icy in winter
tip: Follow the marked forest loop anticlockwise so you reach the stadium first — most people turn back at the baths and never see the best-preserved part.
todo: Stadium seats in the pine wood
Cart ruts on the paved road
Üzümlü dastar cloth in the village
rev: Walkers like the shade and the emptiness; the recurring complaints are a steep narrow access road, minimal signage on site and a ticket booth that is often unstaffed.
entry: Small fee — check locally · Museum Pass usually accepted
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Fethiye and 20 km northeast to Üzümlü, then 4 km of steep forest road to the gate

name: Lycian Way (Western Half)
desc: The first 200 kilometres of Türkiye's original long-distance path, from Ovacık above Ölüdeniz along the cliffs through Faralya and Kabak to Sidyma and the Xanthos valley. It is the hardest and most spectacular section: sea on one side, the Boncuk range on the other, and villages where the pension is somebody's spare room.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — summer on the exposed cliffs is dangerous
tip: Carry three litres per person: the springs marked on older maps are unreliable after June, and several villages on this stretch no longer have a shop.
rev: Walkers rate the coastal views as the best in the country, and consistently report vague waymarking after storms, long waterless stretches and ankle-turning limestone.
onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Fethiye and a dolmuş to Ovacık for the western trailhead; luggage transfer companies operate along the route

name: Afyonkarahisar Castle
desc: A fortress on a 226-metre plug of black volcanic rock standing in the middle of the city like a fist. Hittite records mention a stronghold here in the 14th century BC; what survives is mostly Byzantine and Seljuk. Around 700 steps climb it, and from the top the Anatolian plateau flattens out in every direction.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the steps ice over in winter and bake in July
tip: Start the climb an hour before sunset and carry water; there is nothing to buy on the rock and the staircase has no shade at any point.
rev: Locals and visitors agree the view repays the climb, and complain about the sheer number of steps, patchy lighting after dark and almost no interpretation once you are up there.
onward: Afyonkarahisar sits on the Ankara–İzmir rail line with high-speed services nearby; the rock is a 15-minute walk from the old town

name: Afyonkarahisar
desc: A plateau city of Ottoman timber-framed houses climbing towards the castle rock, with a 13th-century Great Mosque whose flat roof rests on forty wooden columns with carved capitals. It is also the country's dairy and sausage capital: clotted cream with poppy-seed bread for breakfast, sucuk everywhere, and Turkish delight sold by the kilo.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plateau is cold and grey from December to March
tip: Do the Ulu Cami and the Ottoman lanes below the rock in the morning, then eat kaymak with ekmek kadayıf at one of the old shops on the main avenue.
rev: Travellers stopping between Ankara and İzmir are surprised by the food and the mosque, and note that the modern city is drab, the old quarter only partly restored and English rare.
entry: Free — the Ulu Cami has no charge
onward: İzmir (ADB) or Ankara (ESB) then about 3 hours by road; the Ankara–İzmir trains and the high-speed station make it an easy rail stop

name: Ayazini
desc: A village built into and around soft tuff, with Phrygian rock tombs carrying carved lions, Byzantine cave churches whose domes are cut from the living rock, and fairy chimneys standing in the fields behind the houses. It is Cappadocia's geology at a tenth of the scale and a hundredth of the visitor numbers.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plateau is snowy and bleak in midwinter
tip: The best cave church, the one with a carved dome and columns, is behind the village on the far side of the outcrop, not the one signposted from the car park.
todo: Rock-cut church with a carved dome
rev: Visitors are startled that a site like this is empty and free, and mention loose rock, no barriers above drops, no facilities and almost no explanatory signage.
onward: Afyonkarahisar, then 30 km north on the Eskişehir road via İhsaniye; you need a car, because buses are rare

name: Aslantaş and Yılantaş
desc: Two Phrygian rock-cut tombs in the valley near Döğer. Aslantaş has a pair of lions carved facing each other over the doorway, taller than a person and still crisp after 2,600 years; Yılantaş collapsed long ago and lies broken in the field. They stand alone in farmland with no fence and no ticket office.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the dirt approach turns to mud after rain
tip: They are fifteen minutes apart on unpaved farm tracks with almost no signs, so pin both locations before you leave mobile coverage in İhsaniye.
rev: The few who find them describe the lions as extraordinary and the experience as entirely unmanaged: no signs, no guard, farm tracks, and livestock grazing around the monuments.
onward: Afyonkarahisar, then 45 km north towards Döğer; a car is essential and the final stretch is farm track

name: Seydiler Fairy Chimneys
desc: A cluster of tuff pinnacles and mushroom rocks on the edge of Seydiler village, with a rock-cut Phrygian shrine and cave dwellings hollowed into the base of the cliffs. Storks nest on the poles above, tractors cross the field in front, and there is not a single souvenir stall anywhere.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the poppy fields around İhsaniye flower in June
tip: Walk round behind the pinnacles to the cave houses; the front row you see from the road is the least interesting part of the formation.
rev: People arriving from Cappadocia find it modest but genuinely deserted; the recurring notes are no signage, no facilities and a village where asking directions is the only way to find the path.
onward: Afyonkarahisar, then 35 km north via İhsaniye; the Phrygian Valley road links it to Ayazini and Döğer

name: Phrygian Way
desc: A waymarked long-distance trail linking the Phrygian rock monuments across Afyonkarahisar, Kütahya and Eskişehir, through tuff valleys, altar-topped outcrops and villages that still thresh with horses. The Afyon sections around Ayazini and Döğer are the most spectacular and the least walked, marked in the same red and white as the Lycian Way.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plateau bakes in July and snows in winter
tip: Villages on this route have no pensions and often no shop, so arrange a bed in advance through the İhsaniye or Döğer muhtar, or carry a tent and your own water.
rev: Walkers praise the emptiness and the monuments, and warn that the logistics are hard: sparse waymarking in places, no accommodation, dogs at village edges and very little English.
onward: Afyonkarahisar or Kütahya by train or bus, then a taxi out to İhsaniye, Ayazini or Döğer for the trailheads

name: Sandıklı Hüdai Thermal Springs
desc: Afyonkarahisar sits on one of the strongest thermal fields in the country, and Hüdai near Sandıklı is its oldest bath: water near 68 °C, a hot mud pool, and a strip of spa hotels where Turkish families come for two-week cures rather than weekends. Unglamorous, cheap by European standards, and taken entirely seriously.
season: Oct–Apr is the season — locals consider soaking here in summer pointless
tip: Use the municipal bath rather than a hotel spa if you only want a soak; it costs a fraction and the water comes from exactly the same source.
todo: Soak in the hot mud pool
Municipal bath instead of a hotel
rev: Regulars swear by the water for joints and rheumatism; first-timers mention dated hotels, a strong mineral smell, single-sex bathing hours and a medical rather than leisure atmosphere.
entry: ≈₺200–350 (≈€5–8) for the municipal baths; hotels charge more
onward: Afyonkarahisar, then 65 km southwest to Sandıklı and 5 km on to the spa village; regular minibuses from Afyon otogar

name: Kütahya
desc: The tile town: potters have worked here since the 14th century and still do, so façades, fountains and the clock tower are covered in blue and white. Below a Byzantine and Germiyanid castle sit lanes of restored Ottoman konaks, the Great Mosque, and workshops where underglaze painting is still done by hand.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — winters are cold, wet and long at 970 metres
tip: Buy from the workshops in the Germiyan Sokak lanes rather than the shops on the main square, and ask whether a piece is hand-painted or transfer-printed, because both are sold.
todo: Tile Museum in the İmaret complex
rev: Visitors like the tiles and the restored lanes, and note that the rest of the city is ordinary, that many souvenir tiles are machine-printed, and that most sights close by five.
entry: Tile Museum ≈₺100 (≈€2.50); the old lanes are free
onward: Kütahya is on the Ankara–İzmir rail line and about 3 hours by road from Bursa; Zafer (KZR) airport 50 km away has limited flights

name: Aizanoi
desc: The best-preserved Temple of Zeus in Anatolia stands in a village 60 kilometres from Kütahya, raised over a vaulted underground chamber you can still walk into. Beside it are a combined theatre and stadium, a colonnaded market building carrying Diocletian's price edict, two bath houses and a second-century bridge still taking traffic.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plateau is bleak and often snowbound in winter
tip: Go down into the vaulted basement under the temple cella; it is unlit, the entrance on the north side is easy to miss, and it is the oldest part of the building.
todo: Vaulted chamber under the Temple of Zeus
Roman price edict in the macellum
rev: Everyone is astonished by how complete the temple is and how few people are there; complaints are excavation fencing that blocks parts of the site, thin signage and nowhere to eat in the village.
onward: Kütahya by train or bus, then 60 km southwest to Çavdarhisar; minibuses run from Kütahya otogar a few times a day

name: Domaniç
desc: Beech and fir forest on the ridges where Ertuğrul Gazi's tribe summered before there was an Ottoman state, with Halime Hatun's tomb in the village. The plateau meadows above fill with mushrooms in autumn, the roads run through tunnels of trees, and the whole district has about one small hotel.
season: May–Oct; heavy snow closes the high roads from December to March
tip: The Domaniç–İnegöl road over the mountain is the reason to come; drive it in the second half of October when the beech turns and mist sits in the valleys.
rev: Turkish visitors rate the forest and the Ottoman associations; foreign visitors report almost no infrastructure, no English anywhere and a long drive from any useful airport.
onward: Bursa (YEI) airport, then about 2 hours south via İnegöl; from Kütahya it is 90 km north over the mountain

name: Murat Dağı
desc: A 2,300-metre massif on the Kütahya–Uşak border with black pine forest, alpine meadows and thermal springs at its foot. There is a small ski area with a couple of lifts that locals use, and in summer the yayla meadows above Gediz fill with sheep, cold springs and families cooking beside the road.
season: Jan–Mar for snow, Jun–Sep for the meadows; the shoulder months are mud
tip: The thermal hotel at the base is open year-round and is the only reliable bed on the mountain — the lifts run only when there is snow and enough demand.
rev: Turkish skiers describe it as cheap and uncrowded with short runs and unreliable lifts; summer walkers praise the meadows and warn there are no marked trails or maps.
entry: Free; ski lift passes are cheap, roughly ₺300 (≈€7) a day
onward: Kütahya or Uşak by rail, then to Gediz and 25 km up the mountain road; there is no public transport to the top

name: Simav and Eynal Springs
desc: A market town under Şaphane mountain with water coming out of the ground at Eynal, three kilometres away, hot enough that the town heats its buildings with it. The baths are plain municipal concrete rather than spas, and Simav's lake and the beech forests on Şaphane are what you do between soaks.
season: Oct–Apr for the springs; Jun–Sep for the mountain and the lake
tip: Ask the temperature of a pool before you get in — some of the Eynal baths run far hotter than visitors expect and there is nobody supervising.
todo: Soak at the Eynal municipal baths
rev: Turkish spa-goers rate the water strength highly, and everyone notes the facilities are basic and dated, the town has little else for visitors, and almost nobody speaks English.
onward: Kütahya, then 130 km west by minibus; Balıkesir or İzmir (ADB) are the nearest useful airports, roughly 3 hours away

name: Uşak Archaeological Museum
desc: A small provincial museum holding the Karun Treasure: Lydian gold looted from tumuli near Güre in the 1960s, sold to the Met, and returned in 1993 after a long court fight. The winged seahorse brooch was then stolen by the museum's own director and replaced with a fake, and only came back from Germany in 2012.
season: Year-round; closed Mondays
tip: Ask specifically for the seahorse brooch and the wall paintings lifted from the Aktepe tumulus — both are easy to walk past in a room full of small gold objects.
rev: Visitors find the treasure remarkable and the museum itself small and quickly seen, with limited English labelling and a story the displays badly underplay.
onward: Uşak is on the İzmir–Afyon rail line and has a small airport (USQ) with Istanbul flights; the museum is central

name: Blaundus
desc: A Hellenistic city on a spur almost entirely surrounded by canyon, so the only approach is a narrow neck with the city gate still standing across it. Inside are a temple of Demeter, a stadium, rock-cut tombs in the cliff walls and a Byzantine church, with farmland worked in between the ruins.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plateau hits 40 °C in July and freezes in January
tip: Walk out to the far end of the spur past the last field: the canyon drops away on three sides, and that is the view the city was built for.
todo: Rock tombs in the canyon wall
rev: The handful of visitors call it one of the most dramatically sited ruins in the country, and report no ticket office, no signage, no shade and a village road that needs care after rain.
onward: Uşak (USQ) or the train to Uşak, then 40 km south via Ulubey to Sülümenli; a car is essential

name: Ulubey Canyon
desc: A canyon system cut into the Uşak plateau by the Banaz stream, running for tens of kilometres through soft rock. A glass viewing terrace hangs off the rim, poplars and walnut line the river 150 metres below, and a footpath drops to the water where kingfishers work the shallows.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the descent path is slippery in winter and airless in August
tip: The glass terrace is the postcard, but the path down from the rim to the riverbed is where the canyon actually feels big; allow two hours for the climb back.
rev: People rate the terrace and the scale of the gorge, and complain about a fee for what is essentially a viewpoint, litter at the picnic areas and weekend crowds from Uşak.
entry: ≈₺100 (≈€2.50) per car for the nature park
onward: Uşak (USQ) or the İzmir–Afyon train to Uşak, then 25 km south to Ulubey; minibuses run but not as far as the terrace

name: Clandras Bridge
desc: A single-arch bridge over the Banaz stream in the Ulubey canyon, built from large dressed blocks and generally dated to the Phrygian or Lydian period, which would make it one of the oldest bridges still standing anywhere. A Roman aqueduct channel runs along the top, and farm traffic still crosses it.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the river road can flood in late winter
tip: Go down under the arch on the north bank to see the block-work and the aqueduct channel; from the roadway above it looks like an ordinary farm bridge.
todo: Swim in the pool below the arch
rev: Visitors are surprised such an old structure is unfenced and unattended, and report a rough unsigned approach road, no information board and rubbish left by picnickers.
onward: Uşak, then 45 km south via Karahallı; a car is essential and the last few kilometres are gravel

name: Hamam Boğazı, Banaz
desc: A hot spring in a gorge outside Banaz where mineral water around 40 °C fills open pools cut into the rock beside the stream, with a bath building above them. Locals come with towels and food and stay all afternoon; in winter the steam fills the whole gorge and there is snow on the rocks around the pools.
season: Oct–Apr is the point — soaking here in a plateau summer makes no sense
tip: Bathing is single-sex by session, so check the day's timetable at the gate rather than turning up as a couple and being sent away.
todo: Open-air rock pools in winter steam
rev: Turkish visitors rate the water and the setting, and consistently mention basic changing huts, no lockers, crowded weekends and facilities that have not been updated in decades.
onward: Uşak, then 40 km east to Banaz on the Afyon road; minibuses from Uşak otogar, then a taxi out to the springs
